critic_changes: Opened all three cited PDFs (IMF CR 15/282, CDB Country Engagement Strategy 2026-30, CDB Country Economic Review 2022) and extracted their text: every original quote was found on its page. Dates confirmed: IMF report dated October 2015 on its cover; the strategy dated September 2026 (considered by the Board on 30 September 2026); the Country Economic Review 2022 dated 6 November 2023 on the caribank.org economic reviews listing (the PDF shows no date).

Headline: 'a crisis decade under outside rule' overstated the sources (the IMF describes the UK takeover after the 2009 crisis, not a decade of outside rule); rewritten and kept under 160 characters (159).

Arc: 'credits ... fast population growth from migration' as a cause of growth was not supported (the strategy reports the population grew through migration, not that this drove growth); replaced with the review's own account of a tourism-led recovery as COVID-19 restrictions eased, with construction adding to it. The pandemic sentence now attributes the 2020 fall to the year, not as a sourced cause. All arc numbers checked against desk/data/TCA.json (-2.0, 11.6, 22.8, 67.6, 35.6, 27.2, 12.6, 12.9, 4.9, peak 2024) and kept.

Thread 'Hurricanes, then the pandemic': 'the pandemic then shut tourism in 2020' was not supported by any cited passage, and the easing of travel limits was not in the quoted passage; text reworded and a third citation added from the same review ('bolstered by the easing of COVID-19 restrictions').

Thread 'Surpluses and almost no debt': dropped 'These buffers set the territory apart from most of its neighbours', which no cited passage supports; added the IMF passage that supports surpluses since 2012 ('Since the crisis years').
Thread 'A fast-growing population': the causal sentence reworded as plain arithmetic so it does not contradict the tension.

growth_story.headline: After the 2009 crisis and years of decline, tourism-led growth lifted income per person to a record in 2024, though an unexplained 2017 jump drives much of it.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in the Turks and Caicos Islands shrank by 2.0 percent a year in 2008–2016, then grew by 11.6 percent a year in 2017–2024, reaching its highest level yet in 2024. The first era opened with a fall of 22.8 percent in 2009, when the IMF says the global financial crisis, Hurricane Ike and the discovery of government financial mismanagement hit at once, and the United Kingdom took over governance. Austerity from 2012 kept the recovery slow, though growth turned positive again in 2014–2016. The second era's average rests heavily on a 67.6 percent jump in 2017, the year Hurricanes Irma and Maria struck; income per person then fell by 35.6 percent in 2020, the year of the pandemic, before rising by 27.2, 12.6 and 12.9 percent in 2021–2023. The Caribbean Development Bank describes a recovery led by tourism as COVID-19 restrictions eased, with building work adding to it, and growth slowed to 4.9 percent in 2024.

threads.title: Crisis and outside rule
threads.text: In 2009 the economy was hit by the global financial crisis, Hurricane Ike and the discovery of severe financial mismanagement by the territory's government. The United Kingdom took over governance and imposed austerity, which the IMF says held back the recovery from 2012.

growth_story.tension: The data show income per person jumping 67.6 percent in 2017, from 30,183 to 50,586 dollars, yet the sources describe 2017 as a year of severe hurricane damage, not a boom, and none of them explains the jump. In 2021 and 2022, too, the data show income per person up 27.2 and 12.6 percent, while the Caribbean Development Bank reports slower growth in total output in both years, even though the population was rising.
